extra.message: The role_required decorator raises PermissionDenied with a message that explicitly enumerates the allowed roles: "This action requires one of: hr_admin, manager, payroll_specialist" etc. This discloses to an unauthorized user the exact set of roles that would grant access to a resource, providing attackers with intelligence about role-based access control boundaries.

The PortalLoginView (line 54) handles login form validation at lines 59-81 but has no rate limiting on authentication attempts. An attacker can submit unlimited username/password combinations to brute-force credentials for any user account. The view logs login failures via audit_record, but does not throttle, lock out, or CAPTCHA after repeated failures.

The PortalPasswordResetView (line 101) handles password reset requests at lines 108-117 with no rate limiting. An attacker can submit unlimited password reset requests to: (1) enumerate which email addresses have accounts by observing timing differences or response behaviors, and (2) flood users' inboxes with password reset emails, causing annoyance or denial of service.

The PortalPasswordResetConfirmView (password reset token submission) has no rate limiting. An attacker who obtains a valid password reset token can attempt to brute-force the token or simply spam submission requests.
The profile_view POST handler updates user profile information (name, email) with no rate limiting. A state-changing endpoint without throttling can be abused for data alteration spam.

The change_password_view endpoint has no rate limiting. While this requires authentication, an attacker with a stolen session could rapidly attempt to change the password, or a logged-in user could be coerced into changing password repeatedly.

The invite_create POST handler creates new invites (sending emails) with no rate limiting. An HR admin could be coerced or tricked into creating mass invites, or an attacker who compromises an HR admin session could spam invites.

The invite_accept endpoint (invite-based registration) has no rate limiting. An attacker can rapidly attempt to create accounts using invite tokens, or brute-force the token if it's predictable. This is an account registration endpoint.

The admin_user_edit POST handler modifies user accounts (role, active status) with no rate limiting. While protected by hr_admin_required, there's no throttling on this sensitive state-changing operation.
The admin_user_toggle_active POST handler enables/disables user accounts with no rate limiting. Rapid toggling could be used for harassment or disruption.

The audit log service's record() function persists user-controlled data (target_label, user_agent) directly into the audit log without sanitization or encoding for log injection. While the audit log is stored in a structured database field (not a plain text file), an attacker can inject newlines or other control characters via the login form's username field (accounts/views.py:72-80) or via HTTP User-Agent headers. This data reaches the sink at audit/services.py:28-39 where AuditLog.objects.create() stores it.
The change_request_create POST handler creates compensation change requests with no rate limiting. This is a sensitive financial state-changing endpoint.
The change_request_manager_decide POST handler processes manager-level approvals/rejections of compensation changes with no rate limiting. This is a sensitive financial workflow decision endpoint.

The change_request_hr_decide POST handler processes HR-level approvals of compensation changes with no rate limiting. This is the most sensitive financial workflow endpoint that creates immutable compensation records.
The document_upload POST handler allows HR/payroll to upload documents with no rate limiting. An attacker can fill storage with unlimited documents.
The employee_document_upload POST handler allows employees to upload their own documents with no rate limiting. An attacker can fill storage with unlimited files from a compromised employee account.
The document_delete POST handler allows HR/payroll to delete documents with no rate limiting. Documents could be rapidly deleted in a destructive attack.

The EmployeeProfile model stores sensitive Personally Identifiable Information (PII) in plaintext CharField/DateField columns without encryption at rest. Fields include: date_of_birth (line 83), national_id_last4 (line 84), bank_account_last4 (line 85), home_address (line 86), phone (line 87), and emergency_contact (line 88). These are full PII values (date_of_birth, home_address, phone, emergency_contact) or partial identifiers (national_id_last4, bank_account_last4) stored in cleartext in the database. A database compromise would expose all this PII in readable form.

The employee_detail view passes the full EmployeeProfile model instance (which has a foreign key to the User model) to the template context. The User model contains the password hash field ('password'). Any template expression like {{ employee.user.password }} would render the password hash to the page, and it's accessible in the JavaScript context and browser memory.
The employee creation endpoint creates new EmployeeProfile records. There is no rate limiting.
The employee edit endpoint modifies employee profiles. There is no rate limiting.

The `self_change_request_create` view creates ProfileChangeRequest objects and sends notifications to all HR admins. There is no rate limiting on this endpoint, allowing an attacker to flood HR with change requests and notifications.

The field_name from the submitted form is used directly in getattr(profile, field_name, '') to retrieve the old value. While this is validated by the form and later checked against SELF_REQUESTABLE_FIELDS during approval, the getattr at creation time could access any attribute on the profile.
The `self_change_request_decide` view processes approval/rejection decisions for profile change requests. There is no rate limiting on this POST endpoint, allowing rapid approval/rejection cycling.

The PENDING status check (line 272) reads the object outside the atomic transaction (line 276). Two concurrent approving requests could both see PENDING status, leading to double-approval of the same change request.
The department creation endpoint creates new departments. There is no rate limiting.
The department deletion endpoint deletes departments via POST. There is no rate limiting.
The CSV import endpoint processes uploaded files and creates/updates database records. There is no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to repeatedly upload CSVs and flood the database.

The `import_workflow` view renders a list of error strings (`errors`) that contain user-controlled CSV data (field values from the uploaded file). If the `import_result.html` template renders these errors without escaping (e.g., using `|safe`), it could result in stored XSS. Note: Django templates auto-escape by default, but this is a potential XSS sink if the template uses `|safe`.

The _export_payroll function writes CSV cell values (employee display_name, department name, manager display_name) without sanitizing cells that begin with '=', '+', '-', or '@'. When exported CSV is opened in spreadsheet software (Excel, LibreOffice Calc, Google Sheets), these cells can be interpreted as formulas, leading to arbitrary formula execution.

The _export_onboarding function writes CSV cell values (employee display_name, task title, status, reviewed_by username) without sanitizing cells that begin with '=', '+', '-', or '@'. These values can contain user-controlled content that could be interpreted as spreadsheet formulas.

The _export_policy_acks function writes CSV cell values (employee display_name, policy code, policy title) without sanitizing cells that begin with '=', '+', '-', or '@'. Policy titles and employee display names can contain user-managed content that could be interpreted as spreadsheet formulas.
The 'packet_ref' GET parameter is concatenated with BASE_EXPORT_DIR to construct a file path for reading. An attacker can include '../' sequences to read arbitrary files on the system.

The `payroll_fold_drop_014` function reads files from disk using a user-controlled filename (`packet_ref` GET parameter) joined with `BASE_EXPORT_DIR`. An attacker can use `../` sequences to traverse outside the intended directory and read arbitrary files on the system.

The `payroll_fold_drop_014` function reads a user-specified file (via path traversal) and loads the entire content into memory with no size limit. An attacker could request a large file (e.g., /dev/urandom on some systems, or a large log file) to exhaust server memory.
The 'url' GET parameter is passed directly to urllib.request.urlopen(). An attacker can make the server send HTTP requests to arbitrary internal or external hosts, including cloud metadata endpoints.

The `payroll_broker_tile_015` function takes a user-controlled URL from the `url` GET parameter and makes an HTTP request to it using `urllib.request.urlopen()`. This allows server-side request forgery — an attacker can make the server access internal services (e.g., cloud metadata endpoints, internal APIs, database interfaces).

The `payroll_delta_124` function takes user-supplied `amount` and `state` parameters and applies them to the ledger without validation. An attacker can arbitrarily modify the balance and state of the ledger.
The endpoint accepts arbitrary JSON from the request body and allows setting the 'state' field from user input via payload.get('state'). An attacker can manipulate the ledger state.
The endpoint accepts client-controlled 'state' and 'amount' values that modify a server-side ledger. An attacker can manipulate the ledger balance and state to unauthorized values.

The 'amount' parameter is extracted from user input and used in a balance subtraction without any positive/negative bounds checking. A negative amount inverts the operation (adds to balance instead of subtracting), enabling theft.
The 'state' field in the ledger object is set directly from user-controlled input without validation against allowed states.

The endpoint accepts arbitrary pickled data from the request body or GET 'blob' parameter and deserializes it with pickle.loads(). Pickle deserialization of untrusted data leads to arbitrary code execution.

User-controlled request body (or GET parameter 'blob') is deserialized using Python's pickle.loads() without any validation. Pickle deserialization of untrusted data leads to arbitrary code execution.
User-controlled data from request body or GET parameter 'blob' is passed directly to pickle.loads(). Pickle deserialization of untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution.

The `payroll_workset_rebind_194` function merges user-supplied JSON payload directly into the workset dictionary using `workset.update(payload)`. This allows the caller to overwrite any internal field including `role`, `tier`, `approved`, and `balance`.

The endpoint accepts arbitrary JSON from the request body and uses workset.update(payload) to overwrite internal state fields including 'role', 'tier', 'approved', and 'balance'. An attacker can escalate their role or approve transactions.

The `payroll_workset_rebind_194` function takes a user-controlled JSON payload and applies it directly to a dict via `.update()` without any validation of which fields can be set. The response includes the full workset including the `approved` flag.

The endpoint merges client-controlled JSON payload into a 'workset' dict that defines role, tier, and approval state. An attacker can set arbitrary values for 'role', 'approved', and other security-sensitive fields.

The entire JSON request payload (or POST data) is used to update the 'workset' dictionary which controls role, tier, approval status, and balance. An attacker can set themselves as admin or approve their own records.

The 'expr' GET parameter is passed directly to Python's eval() function. Despite attempts to restrict builtins, this can still be bypassed (e.g., via attribute access on literals like (1).__class__.__mro__) to achieve arbitrary code execution.
User-controlled 'expr' parameter from GET request is passed to Python's built-in eval() function. Although __builtins__ is set to {}, there are well-known bypass techniques to escape restricted eval.

The endpoint sets a cookie 'portal_crumb' using response.set_cookie() without specifying Secure=True, HttpOnly=True, or SameSite. The cookie can be accessed by JavaScript and transmitted over unencrypted HTTP.

The `payroll_crumb_lane_290` function sets a cookie named `portal_crumb` with a value taken directly from the `marker` GET parameter. The cookie has no HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite flags set. An attacker could inject arbitrary values into the cookie via the URL parameter.
User-controlled 'marker' GET parameter is set directly as a cookie value with no sanitization. No httponly, secure, or samesite attributes are set on the cookie.

The `payroll_crumb_lane_290` function sets a cookie named `portal_crumb` with user-controlled content from the `marker` GET parameter, without setting `httponly`, `secure`, or `samesite` attributes. This cookie can be accessed by JavaScript and transmitted over unencrypted connections.

The `payroll_identity_ping_336` function is the only payroll operations endpoint that lacks the `_wrk_gate` authentication check. It accepts GET and POST requests without any authentication, processing arbitrary user-controlled `handle` and `channel` parameters.
The endpoint contains hardcoded verifier credentials: 'north' -> '4812' and 'south' -> '5930'. These are static credentials embedded in source code that authenticate identity handle lookups.

The `payroll_identity_hint_363` function uses hardcoded verifier values `{'north': '4812', 'south': '5930'}` for authentication. These static credentials are the same across all deployments and can be easily discovered through source code access.

The `payroll_origin_mirror_373` function reflects the `Origin` request header directly in the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header and sets `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. This allows any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to this endpoint, bypassing same-origin policy.

The Origin header from the request is reflected as Access-Control-Allow-Origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is set to 'true'. This allows any arbitrary website to make credentialed cross-origin requests.

The `payroll_jinja_cast_384` function takes a `fragment` parameter from user GET input and renders it through Jinja2's Template class. An attacker can inject Jinja2 template expressions like `{{ config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read() }}` to achieve RCE.

The 'fragment' GET parameter is directly concatenated into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. An attacker can inject Jinja2 template expressions that execute arbitrary Python code via Jinja2's sandbox bypass techniques.
User-controlled 'fragment' GET parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template source string, then rendered. This allows server-side template injection leading to RCE.
User-controlled 'fragment' parameter from GET request is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 Template string and rendered. This allows Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI), leading to RCE.

The 'name' GET parameter is concatenated with BASE_EXPORT_DIR to construct a file path for writing. An attacker can include '../' sequences to write files to arbitrary locations outside the intended directory.

User-controlled 'name' parameter is used to construct a file path. The request body is written to this path without sanitization. An attacker can use '../' sequences to write files outside the intended directory.

The 'host' GET parameter is directly concatenated into a shell command string passed to os.system(). An attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands by including shell metacharacters (;, |, &, $(), backticks) in the host parameter.
User-controlled 'host' parameter from GET request is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to os.system(). No sanitization or escaping is performed.

The endpoint accepts arbitrary JSON from the request body and passes it directly (or via the 'filter' key) as a MongoDB query filter. An attacker can inject MongoDB operators ($where, $ne, $regex, $gt) to bypass intended query logic and extract unauthorized data.

The `payroll_mongo_lane_413` function passes user-controlled JSON data directly as a MongoDB query filter without sanitization. An attacker can inject MongoDB operators like `$ne`, `$regex`, `$where`, `$gt`, etc. to manipulate the query logic and bypass intended filtering.

The `payroll_mongo_lane_413` function executes a user-controlled MongoDB query with no pagination or timeout. An attacker could craft an expensive query (e.g., using $regex on unindexed fields) to consume excessive database resources.
The MongoDB connection string defaults to 'mongodb://localhost:27017' with no username/password. If the MONGO_URL env var is not set, the database is accessed without any authentication.

User-controlled JSON payload is used directly as a MongoDB query filter without sanitization. An attacker can inject MongoDB query operators ($ne, $regex, $where, etc.) to bypass intended query logic.

The `payroll_frame_slip_423` function explicitly sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` (disabling XSS filter) and `Content-Security-Policy: ""` (empty, effectively disabling CSP). This weakens browser-side security protections for this endpoint.
The `payroll_frame_slip_423` function explicitly disables XSS protection and Content-Security-Policy headers, weakening browser-side security protections.
The endpoint creates an SSL context with certificate verification disabled (_create_unverified_context()) and uses it to make HTTPS requests. This disables TLS certificate validation.
SSL certificate verification is explicitly disabled using ssl._create_unverified_context() when making an HTTPS request to a remote endpoint.
The endpoint exposes internal configuration values in the response, including the Django settings module name and the base export directory path.

The `payroll_trace_panel_443` function returns the `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE` environment variable and the `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` path in the JSON response. This leaks internal configuration details about the deployment.

The lxml XML parser is configured with load_dtd=True and resolve_entities=True, which enables external entity processing. An attacker can include XML external entities in the request body to read local files, perform SSRF, or cause a denial of service.
XML parser is configured with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False. User-controlled request body is parsed as XML, allowing XML External Entity (XXE) attacks.
When DEBUG is enabled and DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set, the application falls back to a hardcoded secret key 'dev-insecure-key-do-not-use-in-production'.

The database configuration in DATABASES does not specify any SSL/TLS parameters (no sslmode, ssl=True, or similar). Database traffic between the application and PostgreSQL is transmitted in plaintext.

The PostgreSQL database password defaults to 'hr_portal' when the POSTGRES_PASSWORD environment variable is not set. This means deployments that fail to configure the env var will use a weak, hardcoded default password, storing the database credential in plaintext in the settings file.

The database password defaults to 'hr_portal' if the POSTGRES_PASSWORD environment variable is not set. In development environments or any deployment where this env var is omitted, the database is accessible with a known default password.

The PostgreSQL database connection configuration does not enforce SSL/TLS. The `OPTIONS` dict only specifies `connect_timeout` with no SSL parameters. If the database is on a remote host, credentials and data are transmitted in cleartext over the network.
The HR request creation endpoint creates new HRRequest objects and sends notifications to all HR admins. There is no rate limiting.
The HR request comment endpoint creates comments and sends notifications. There is no rate limiting.
The HR request status change endpoint modifies request status and sends notifications. There is no rate limiting.
The onboarding task creation endpoint creates tasks and sends notifications. There is no rate limiting.
The onboarding task submission endpoint handles file uploads and status changes. There is no rate limiting.
The onboarding task review endpoint changes task status and sends notifications. There is no rate limiting.
The policy acknowledgement endpoint creates acknowledgement records. There is no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly create many acknowledgement records.
The policy creation endpoint creates new policies with version history. There is no rate limiting.
The policy edit endpoint changes policies and optionally bumps versions. There is no rate limiting.

The WebhookForm's `clean_target_url` method uses an exact-match denylist to block localhost and internal IPs. This can be trivially bypassed using alternative representations: `127.1` (short form of 127.0.0.1), `0x7f.0x0.0x0.0x1` (hex), `2130706433` (integer), DNS names that resolve to internal IPs, or `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]` (IPv4-mapped IPv6).

The WebhookEndpoint model stores the 'secret' field as a plain CharField (max_length=128) with no encryption or hashing. This shared secret used for HMAC-signing webhook payloads is stored in cleartext in the database, making it accessible to anyone with database read access.

The fire_webhook function writes webhook delivery details including target_url, event data, and HMAC signature to a local log file (WEBHOOK_DELIVERY_LOG). This log contains sensitive integration secrets.

The `fire_webhook` function writes webhook delivery details to a local log file. The logged data includes `endpoint.target_url` which is user-controlled (set during webhook creation). If the URL contains newline characters or other log-injection sequences, an attacker can forge log entries to mislead auditors or inject malicious content into the log.

The `whoami` view uses `@csrf_exempt` which disables CSRF protection on a GET endpoint that supports session cookie authentication. Though GET endpoints are typically read-only, CSRF via GET could potentially leak authenticated user data cross-origin through techniques like `` or `` tags, combined with error-based side channels.

The `employees_list` view uses `@csrf_exempt` which disables CSRF protection. This GET endpoint supports session cookie authentication and returns employee data. CSRF via GET could potentially leak employee data cross-origin.

The `employee_detail` view uses `@csrf_exempt` which disables CSRF protection. This GET endpoint supports session cookie authentication and returns detailed employee data including potentially sensitive internal notes for HR admins.
The `my_compensation` view uses `@csrf_exempt` which disables CSRF protection. This GET endpoint supports session cookie authentication and returns compensation data (salary, bonus).
The `documents_list` view uses `@csrf_exempt` which disables CSRF protection. This GET endpoint supports session cookie authentication and returns document metadata.
The `policies_list` view uses `@csrf_exempt` which disables CSRF protection. This GET endpoint supports session cookie authentication and returns policy data.

The `receive_test_webhook` endpoint is labeled as a 'Local-only stub' but is NOT guarded behind any debug flag, configuration toggle, or environment check. It is accessible on any authenticated POST request to the endpoint. Debug endpoints left accessible in production can leak application topology, accept unexpected data, and provide attackers with an unhardened reflection/echo surface. The docstring says 'Local-only stub: developers can POST here to verify the API surface' yet no runtime guard (e.g., `if not settings.DEBUG: return 404`) exists.

The `receive_test_webhook` view uses `@csrf_exempt` which disables Django's CSRF protection on a POST endpoint that accepts JSON. This endpoint also supports session cookie authentication via `_auth_user_for_json`. A CSRF attack could trick an authenticated user (via session cookie) into making an unintended POST request to this endpoint, echoing attacker-controlled JSON data. While the impact is limited (only echoes data back), the combination of `@csrf_exempt` with session-based auth on a POST endpoint is a CSRF vulnerability.

The `receive_test_webhook` view at lines 202-213 accepts POST requests from any authenticated user, parses JSON, and echoes it back with no rate limiting. An attacker could send unlimited POST requests to this endpoint, consuming server resources (CPU for JSON parsing, memory, bandwidth).

The `api_key_create` view at lines 227-257 handles POST requests to create new API keys with no rate limiting. An authenticated user can create an unlimited number of API keys in rapid succession, potentially exhausting database storage and enabling downstream abuse of the API key system.

The ALLOWED_UPLOAD_CONTENT_TYPES set includes 'application/octet-stream' (line 29), a generic catch-all MIME type that any file can claim. This completely undermines the content-type validation in validate_upload() (line 60-62) because an attacker can upload arbitrary file types (executables, scripts, HTML files) simply by setting the Content-Type header to 'application/octet-stream'. The allowlist check becomes a no-op.

The `ALLOWED_UPLOAD_CONTENT_TYPES` set includes `application/octet-stream` (line 29), which is a generic binary content type. Since any binary file can claim this content type, this effectively bypasses the content-type validation in `validate_upload()`. An attacker could upload arbitrary file types (executables, scripts, etc.) by setting the Content-Type to application/octet-stream.

A hardcoded weak password `DEMO_PASSWORD = "password-1234"` is defined and used to create all demo user accounts in the seed data management command. This password is embedded directly in source code and is the same for every account created by this command.

The AuditContextMiddleware stores the raw HTTP_USER_AGENT header value in the thread-local audit context with only a 255-character length truncation (line 26). No sanitization is applied to remove control characters such as newlines (\n, \r), carriage returns, or other characters that could inject fake entries into the audit trail. If the audit service writes these values to a text-based log format, an attacker can forge audit log entries by crafting a malicious User-Agent header containing log-delimiting sequences.

The `notification_mark_read` view uses Django's `redirect()` function on the `note.link` field (line 169-170). Django's `redirect()` will redirect to any URL including external ones. While the `link` field is currently populated from trusted application code with relative paths (e.g., `/onboarding/{task.id}/`), there is no validation that the link is a safe internal URL. If a notification's `link` field were to ever contain an external URL (via a future code change, database manipulation, or other vulnerability), this would become an open redirect vulnerability.

The template renders {{ n.link }} inside an href attribute without URL scheme sanitization. Django's autoescaping escapes HTML characters (like <, >, ") but does NOT validate or sanitize URL schemes. If the n.link value is user-controllable (e.g., stored from user input via a form or API), an attacker could set it to javascript:alert(document.cookie) or similar malicious JavaScript URLs. When a victim user clicks the 'Open' link on the notification, the JavaScript executes in the application's origin context, bypassing Django's autoescaping because the escaping only handles HTML entities, not URL protocol validation.
